style: Read clearly and naturally, at a moderate pace
lines: Welcome to Millbrook. Every one of these dots knows how they feel about a new skate park. You only get to ask some of them.
Pick who you ask, how you ask, and how many. Then run the poll and read your headline.
One poll can be lucky. Run the same design fifty more times and see where the results land.
Here is the truth. A fair method scatters around it. A biased one lands off to the side, and more people will not move it back.
The plus or minus only covers the luck of the draw. It says nothing about who you left out.
In nineteen thirty six, a magazine polled more than two million people and still called the election wrong. Let's see why.
Same town, same number of people. The only difference is who got asked.
The Millbrook Courier has ten thousand dollars for a poll. Spend it on the design you trust most.
This one is close. Think about how small your plus or minus needs to be.
Published. Let's see how it held up.
Pick who you ask, then press Run poll.
Try Run fifty more like this, then Reveal the truth.
More people will not fix this. Try n equals two thousand and see.
A fair method scatters around the truth. Now try a biased method, or a leaning question, and compare.
Run the Digest's method, then a fair method. Each button runs twenty polls of two thousand people in Millbrook.
Now run the other one. Same town, same two thousand people per poll.
Same number of people, two piles. Compare each pile and its plus or minus with the truth line.
Design a poll that costs ten thousand dollars or less, then Publish. One poll per round, and the truth stays hidden until then.
Check your two results, then press Next round.
Three rounds done. Read your round log, or Start over with new towns.
